title: Evaluation of Automotive Battery Modules Using a Coupled Numerical Model With Hybrid Passive–Active Thermal Management
abstract: ABSTRACT The increasing deployment of lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs) in electric vehicles (EVs) demands robust thermal management to ensure safety and performance, particularly, under high‐current discharge and dynamic load conditions. The present study evaluated a battery pack at the system level, using both detailed finite‐volume simulation and system‐level dynamic modeling for an LFP battery module. Initially, a 3D thermal model was developed to evaluate the effectiveness of phase change material (PCM)‐based passive battery thermal management systems (BTMS). Under 5C discharge, the 4S1P module's peak temperature dropped from 72°C to 44.8°C through progressive integration of varying PCM layer thickness from 2 to 8 mm, enhancing the varied convective heat transfer coefficient, and ultimately incorporating metal foam within the PCM matrix. To evaluate the system under real‐world EV operating conditions, a Simulink model was developed using an identical module configuration and thermal parameters, incorporating a liquid cooling strategy using water as the coolant, enabling effective heat extraction across both FTP‐75 and UDDS drive cycles at varying ambient temperatures from 25°C to 40°C and different Reynolds numbers (Re). Under the stringent FTP‐75 drive cycle at 40°C ambient, the model demonstrated robust thermal performance, with Re = 3000 resulting in a peak temperature of 42°C, while increasing coolant flow at Re = 10 000 reduced it to 38.5°C. In comparison, the milder UDDS cycle yielded a peak of 41.8°C at Re = 3000 and 39.3°C at Re = 10 000. The present study demonstrates battery pack‐to‐system thermal synergy and provides a validated framework for efficient BTMS design in EVs.
title_zh: Evaluation of Automotive Battery Modules Using a Coupled Numerical Model With Hybrid Passive–Active Thermal Management

title: Development of a physics-based electrochemical and thermal model of Li-ion batteries for microcontroller applications
abstract: Enabling fast-charging procedures is one of the key challenges of Li-ion battery applications, from automotive topower tools. A promising strategy for realizing reliable fast-charging algorithms in battery systems involves employingmodel-based estimations of internal cell states and integrating these predictions into the charging control.Utilizing this approach to simulate cells during charging reduces the risk of plating, thereby enhancing safety as wellas cycle stability. However, achieving accurate model predictions requires substantial computational effort and extensiveparameterization, making onboard application on a simple battery management system (BMS) challenging. Toaddress this gap, a reduced physicochemical and thermal model is developed capable of running on a basic microcontroller(MCU). This model comprises the electrochemical processes, including the anode potential, which enablesthe detection of lithium plating. Combined with the thermal model, it also considers the cell’s thermal behavior andtemperature-driven parameter changes.
title_zh: Development of a physics-based electrochemical and thermal model of Li-ion batteries for microcontroller applications

title: Model for optimal sizing of Photovoltaic and Battery Energy Storage Systems considering an efficient scheme for contracted power capacity
abstract: This paper presents a novel optimization model for the simultaneous sizing of photovoltaic (PV) systems and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in behind-the-meter (BTM) self-consumption applications. The proposed formulation maximizes the project’s Net Present Value (NPV) from a prosumer perspective by integrating optimal battery scheduling with active energy trading strategies in the electricity market. The core contribution of the proposal is the determination of the optimal hourly contracted power capacity, providing a granular approach to managing grid connection costs. The inclusion of an adequate power demand contracting scheme has been overlooked on existing PV & BESS sizing optimization models. The performance of the model is validated against a well-known sizing approach with a case study involving a 6000 kWp PV, a 17000 kWh BESS for a 1000 kW data center in Madrid yielding a Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) of 114 US $ /MWh. In contrast, the proposed model recommends a six-period power contracting scheme of [0,0,0,0,0,1] MW for a 6100 kWp (PV system) and a significantly smaller 9330 kWh (BESS), achieving an Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of 12.7% and a reduced LCOE of 77.5 US $ /MWh. We highlight that the Net Present Value of the project is significantly improved from US $ -9,135,410.60 (negative) to US $ 3,623,548 (positive) indicating, that energy/demand charges savings effectively offset both CAPEX and OPEX while generating additional profit. The inclusion of optimal power contracting schemes in the optimization model enhances the net present value by 24.6% compared to an optimized scenario that lacks strategic management of demand capacity charges.
title_zh: Model for optimal sizing of Photovoltaic and Battery Energy Storage Systems considering an efficient scheme for contracted power capacity
